title: Dan Hernandez Answered Slocum’s Calls for 28 Years. East Texas Remembers His Service
summary: Slocum Fire Safety Chief Dan Hernandez served his neighbors as a volunteer firefighter for 28 years and suffered a fatal medical emergency while responding to a July brush fire.
content:
For 28 years, Dan Louis Hernandez Jr. answered emergency calls for neighbors in and around Slocum. His last response came July 7, when the Slocum Volunteer Fire Department’s safety chief went to a brush fire and suffered a cardiovascular event at the scene. Hernandez died four days later, on July 11, at age 71.

The U.S. Fire Administration’s 2026 firefighter-fatality search lists Hernandez by name, location and date of death and notes that its information is provisional. A U.S. First Responders Association fatality notice identifies him as a volunteer with 28 years of service and gives the July 7 incident and July 11 death dates. KLTV and KETK independently reported the department’s account, and the funeral home’s published obituary confirms his service history and family-approved memorial details.

Those records establish the core facts. They do not tell the full story of 28 years of nights, weekends, training sessions, equipment checks and calls that begin without knowing what the crew will find. Volunteer firefighters protect communities where a fully staffed career department may be distant or financially unrealistic. Their work is local government and neighbor-to-neighbor service at the same time.

Hernandez held the title of Fire Safety Chief with the Slocum Volunteer Fire Department. The department described him as an integral member and longtime friend whose courage, compassion and dedication extended beyond emergency scenes. RepWatchr is attributing those character descriptions to the people who served beside him; they are not labels inferred from an incident report.

The final call was a brush fire. According to the fatality notice, Hernandez experienced a cardiovascular event while at the scene. He was transported to a regional medical center, stabilized and later transferred to another hospital, where he died despite treatment. Local reporting says family, friends and fellow firefighters were with him when he died.

The difference between an incident date and a death date is important in firefighter records. Hernandez’s emergency occurred July 7; his death was July 11. The federal search record and first-responder notice connect those dates, while the obituary confirms his age and long service. RepWatchr found no responsible basis to speculate about medical history, treatment decisions or any other private health detail.

His obituary says Hernandez was known as “Dano,” was born Jan. 27, 1955, and spent more than 28 years protecting his neighbors as a volunteer firefighter. It also remembers a life beyond the station: work in the air-conditioning business, ownership of Bowman’s Country Corner Store in Denson Springs with his late wife Cathy, love for the outdoors, Masonic service and devotion to family. Those details matter because volunteer fire departments are built from people who have ordinary jobs, families and community ties before the pager sounds.

Slocum and the wider Anderson County community honored Hernandez with a firefighter honor-guard service July 17 at Slocum High School. Members of the Slocum Volunteer Fire Department served as pallbearers. The obituary directed memorial gifts to the department in his honor, a request that turns remembrance toward the organization in which he served. Anyone who wants to contribute should use the current contact information in the funeral-home notice or verify it directly with the department before sending money.

Hero stories can become exaggerated if grief is used to fill gaps in the record. Hernandez’s service does not need embellishment. Twenty-eight years as a volunteer firefighter is a long record of showing up. The final documented act was responding to a brush fire. The department’s public statement says he supported fellow firefighters and helped neighbors whenever needed. Those facts are enough to explain why East Texans paused to honor him.

The story also points to a responsibility larger than one tribute. Rural volunteer departments depend on training, safe equipment, medical screening, mutual aid, dispatch systems and enough people to rotate through demanding calls. Recognition should include asking what a department needs before the next emergency, not only after a loss. Residents can support their local department by learning whether it needs volunteers, attending public meetings or fundraisers, and verifying donation channels.

No article can define a person for his family or colleagues. Public records can only preserve the service facts with care. Hernandez was a 71-year-old volunteer safety chief. He served for 28 years. He responded to a brush fire on July 7, suffered a fatal medical emergency and died July 11. His community held an honor-guard service, and his family asked that memorial support go to the Slocum department.

That is a record of commitment measured not in one dramatic moment but in decades. East Texas communities often rely on people willing to leave the dinner table, a job site or a night’s sleep when someone else calls for help. Dan Hernandez was one of those people. Remembering him accurately is one way to honor the promise behind volunteer service: when a neighbor is in danger, someone will answer.
